title: Trump has outsized influence in stock markets, but investors grow wary
summary: Stock markets wrapped up a head-spinning week of trading on a positive note Friday, with tech stocks rallying after taking a beating earlier on.

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump, pictured at Mar-a-Lago on Nov. 26, has repeatedly taken steps to boost the market, announcing deals, truces and agreements to move markets and push stocks higher, but is he reaching his limit? (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Business·Analysis
Stock markets wrapped up a head-spinning week of trading on a positive note Friday, with tech stocks rallying after taking a beating earlier on.
Experts say the Trump effect may have 'started to unwind'
The Nasdaq had its best week in seven months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 both finished the session in positive territory.
When asked Thursday what he was most thankful for, U.S. President Donald Trump told American troops deployed abroad that stock markets have set records 88 times during his presidency.
"We have the highest stock markets in history," said Trump.
Markets have indeed performed incredibly well during Trump's tenure — and the president has played an outsized role in fuelling that rise.

Trump has repeatedly taken steps to boost the market, announcing deals, truces and agreements to move markets and push stocks higher. This week, he made one of his boldest moves yet, intervening to push the board of Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang as CEO.
It led to one of the biggest one-day surges the Nasdaq has ever seen.
What is the 'Trump put?'

Traders call it the "Trump put," a belief that the president will intervene to push markets higher. Whether that's in announcing a deal or truce that may not be quite complete or backing off policies the markets dislike (as he did after the so-called Liberation Day tariffs caused a massive sell off in April 2025.)
But the Trump put was tested this week.

Nvidia lost much of the ground it regained on Monday. The company's stock price rallied briefly on the news that Huang would return to the corner office. But since then it resumed its fall. Since Nvidia peaked on Oct. 6, it has fallen nearly 31 per cent since.
The tech heavy Nasdaq is also down about 13 per cent in the same time period.
That slump has some wondering if Trump is reaching the limit of his ability to move markets.
"It's started to unwind," said Jim Thorne, the chief market strategist at Wellington-Altus Private Wealth.
Trump's Commerce Department under fire as Nvidia CEO scandal continues to rock markets
Part of that is the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections because, Thorne says, Trump moved away from the promises he made to his base.
"Let's be honest and clear about this, right? He screwed up. He lost in the midterms because he got away from the America first affordability crisis," said Thorne in an interview Friday.
But Thorne also says Americans and investors are wary of the way Trump involves himself in the markets.
"Is Trump losing his effect? Yes. People are tired," he said
Is Trump's stock market influence waning?

The whole basis for the Trump put is that investors believe him when he says something will happen. Or that it won't happen. This week he told markets Nvidia would be fine because Huang did nothing wrong.

At a fundamental level, that was hard to completely believe. Huang may not have broken any laws. He may not have known he was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy or that his paramour's company was accused of illegally funnelling the best and most powerful American chips to Chinese companies with ties to the Chinese military.

items: North American stocks soar, recovering half of last week's plunge after Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia's CEO
Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO

blocks.text: Even with Huang back in the CEO's chair, the company will face increased scrutiny and tighter export regulations.
But Richard Dias, the global macro strategist at IceCap Asset Management, says there's a broader fatigue at play.
"Is the Trump thing getting exhausted? I think obviously, yes, I think everyone is exhausted. People who agree with him are exhausted," said Dias.
He says the idea that the president alone could move markets was always a bit of an embellishment.
"I think his weight and power in the markets, I think it's just massively, massively overstated. The markets are way smarter than you or me or any one man," Dias told CBC News in an interview.

Dias says markets were already looking for a reason to move against the broader AI trade. The circular financing agreements (under which NVIDIA would invest in AI companies provided they would in turn buy Nvidia chips) was raising alarm bells. And there were real questions about the sustainability of the AI buildout and focus on (wildly unpopular) data centres.
Data centre backlash is a problem for Trump’s Republicans
Dias says humans love a narrative.

"The story that people will tell ourselves is, 'oh, Jensen Huang's infidelities and Trump meddling will be the cause of this tech sell-off,' when really there was a litany of ready-made examples and reasons why there was already loads of weakness."
There are still plenty of reasons the AI trade will rally.

There are still plenty of forces that may drive markets down — the Federal Reserve is eying more rate hikes before the end of the year that would dampen investor enthusiasm — and it would be folly to underestimate the power of any U.S. president to sway markets.

But there is a growing sentiment that this was the week that Trump began to see his impact tested and many, including the widely read Wall Street newsletter, The Kobeissi Letter, have declared an end to the "Trump put".
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Armstrong is the CBC's senior business correspondent. He was a foreign correspondent and a parliamentary reporter for CBC News. Peter hosted the business program On the Money and World Report on CBC Radio. He is the author of the CBC newsletter Mind Your Business
